# Tuberculosis and undernutrition: improving estimates to reinforce the policy imperative

**Authors:** Matthew J Saunders; Pranay Sinha; J Peter Cegielski; Rebecca A Clark; James A Seddon; Leonardo Martinez; Madhavi Bhargava; Anurag Bhargava; Richard G White; Rein MGJ Houben; C Finn McQuaid

**Affiliations:** 1Institute for Infection and Immunity, City St. George’s, University of London, London, UK | 2Faculty of Public Health and Policy, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, London, UK | 3Boston Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4Section of Infectious Diseases, Department of Medicine, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America. | 5Department of Epidemiology, Rollins School of Public Health, Emory University, Atlanta, USA | 6TB Modelling Group, TB Centre, and Centre for Mathematical Modelling of Infectious Diseases, Department of Infectious Disease Epidemiology, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, London, UK | 7Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom | 8Desmond Tutu TB Centre, Department of Paediatrics and Child Health, Stellenbosch University, Cape Town, South Africa | 9Boston University School of Public Health, Department of Epidemiology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America. | 10Department of Community Medicine, Yenepoya Medical College, Mangalore, Karnataka, India | 11Department of Medicine, Kasturba Medical College Mangalore, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, Karnataka, India | 12Department of Medicine, McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada

Undernutrition is a key driver of the tuberculosis epidemic, increasing the risk of developing tuberculosis and of poor outcomes in those who do so.1 Every year, the World Health Organization (WHO) publishes estimates of the number of tuberculosis episodes attributable to undernutrition and other risk factors, based on population attributable fractions (PAF). These allow stakeholders to compare the relative role of different risk factors in the tuberculosis epidemic, shaping policy and setting research agendas.

In 2023, WHO estimated a PAF of tuberculosis attributable to undernutrition of 17%; but in 2024 this was revised to 8.9%.2,3 Why? Because the two parameters used to calculate the PAF (prevalence of undernutrition and relative risk [RR] of tuberculosis associated with undernutrition) changed. In 2023, undernourishment – an indirect, modelled estimate of the percentage of the population with insufficient per capita energy availability to maintain a normal active and healthy life – was used as the exposure.2 However, the RR estimate used was derived from a systematic review of six studies showing a log-linear, dose-response relationship between body mass index (BMI) and tuberculosis. The RR of 3.2 (95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 3.1–3.3) compared tuberculosis incidence at a BMI of 16.0kg/m2 versus 25.0kg/m2.2,4 In 2024, undernutrition (BMI<18.5kg/m2 in adults) was the exposure, and the RR estimate used was 2.0 (95% CI: 1.7–2.2).3 This was extracted from a meta-analysis of four studies from a 2024 Cochrane review, which aimed to provide a simple binary estimate of the risk of tuberculosis associated with undernutrition versus no undernutrition (BMI≧18.5kg/m2).5

This shift to anthropometric measures is welcome,6 and we recognise WHO’s need for standardised, comparable metrics across risk factors based on systematic reviews addressing bias and heterogeneity. However, the Cochrane review’s approach paradoxically introduced new limitations that suggest the RR estimate used is likely underestimated. First, because of the emphasis on undernutrition as a binary exposure, several studies were excluded, including large cohorts included in the previous review and newer cohorts from settings with a high tuberculosis burden.7 Second, studies done in populations that may have a different RR of tuberculosis associated with undernutrition were inappropriately pooled, including adults and children, people with and without HIV and/or diabetes, and those with rare health conditions (e.g. post-gastrectomy). Third, definitions of undernutrition and particularly comparator groups (i.e. no undernutrition) differed between included studies, leading to classification inconsistencies. Fourth, the review did not adequately consider the previously established dose-response relationship between BMI and tuberculosis, demonstrated again in many of its included studies.8

Small, let alone large, errors in RR are important because the impact on the PAF and number of attributable cases is substantial (Figure 1). Our recent study provides revised and improved estimates using dose-response meta-analysis.9 This shows that tuberculosis risk is highest at the lowest BMI values and decreases non-linearly as BMI increases, with the steepest reduction in risk occurring when moving through underweight and normal weight ranges, and more modest reductions occurring through overweight and obese ranges. From our study, the estimated mean BMIs for people with and without undernutrition globally (i.e. below and above a BMI of 18.5kg/m2) sit at 17.0kg/m2 and 25.6kg/m2, which then gives an RR of 5.0 (95%CI: 4.2–5.9) and a PAF of 28.2%. Comparing 17.0kg/m2 with 21.8kg/m2 (the midpoint of the normal weight BMI category), the RR would be 2.8 (95%CI: 2.5–3.1) and the PAF 15.0%. By addressing the limitations of the previous approach, we show that current RR estimates used by WHO will substantially underestimate the population-level importance of undernutrition for the tuberculosis epidemic.

Consequently, policy decisions and allocation of resources may be directed away from this crucial determinant, leading to missed opportunities and diminished funding for nutritional interventions that could prevent tuberculosis and save lives. To ensure more accurate estimates moving forward, WHO PAF calculations for undernutrition should account for the dose-response relationship between BMI and tuberculosis, as well as the underlying distribution of BMI in different populations.10 To better characterise the relationship between nutrition and tuberculosis, future research should prioritise prospective cohorts with repeated anthropometric measurements using robust methods for tuberculosis diagnosis, particularly in underrepresented groups (e.g. children) from low- and middle-income countries; harmonise data collection protocols across cohorts; and utilise advanced analytical approaches to better account for heterogeneity (e.g. individual participant data meta-analyses, Bayesian hierarchical models).

The importance of undernutrition in driving the tuberculosis epidemic is high and warrants correct estimation. By using improved RR estimates alongside appropriate anthropometric measures, we enhance our understanding of the relative importance of undernutrition and ensure this critical determinant of tuberculosis receives the attention it deserves.
